summary: Looks at issues when a device uses both DHCPv4 and DHCPv6, notably how clients should handle configuration information from both kinds of server when it might conflict. It makes a recommendation. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: What to do when two people give you instructions about the same chore from different books, and they might not agree.

subtitle: How to manage IPv4 and IPv6 configuration when both protocols are in use.

tldr.problem: When a device uses both IPv4 and IPv6 (dual-stack), it needs configuration from both DHCP and DHCPv6 servers. These protocols may return conflicting information—different DNS servers, different NTP servers, incompatible options—and there is no standard way for clients to merge or prioritize the information.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4477 analyzes the issues in detail and proposes solutions. The IETF converged on a two-server approach: run separate DHCP and DHCPv6 servers, with a single database generating consistent configuration for both. Clients merge the responses using best-practice heuristics, and sites maintain consistency at the administrator level.
tldr.outcome: This guidance helped IPv6 deployments manage dual-stack configuration in practice. The two-server approach became the recommended strategy, with the understanding that IPv4 DHCP will likely be needed for many years alongside DHCPv6.

today: RFC 4477 is an Informational RFC that remains current. Its recommendation of the two-server approach with synchronized configuration is how most dual-stack IPv6 deployments operate today.

sections.title: The Dual-Stack Configuration Problem
sections.content:
The original DHCP (RFC 2131) configures IPv4 addresses and related settings. With IPv6's arrival, a new DHCPv6 (RFC 3315) was created for IPv6 configuration. Today, most networks in transition run dual-stack—both IPv4 and IPv6—and devices need configuration from both protocols.

A dual-stack device may need an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address, IPv4 DNS servers, IPv6 DNS servers, NTP servers (which can be reached by either protocol), and a DNS search path. Currently, DHCP returns only IPv4 data, and DHCPv6 returns only IPv6 data. The device must decide how to merge the responses, but there is no standard guidance.

The problem is not new merging in general (networks already merge configuration from multiple sources), but rather the specific challenge that DHCP and DHCPv6 are independent protocols that may not stay synchronized.
sections.plainLanguage: Your router needs to know both its IPv4 address (the old way) and its IPv6 address (the new way). The server that gives out IPv4 info and the server that gives out IPv6 info are separate, and sometimes they disagree about things like which DNS server to use.

sections.title: The Seven Issues
sections.content:
RFC 4477 identifies several problems that arise:

Handling multiple responses: Should a client use the most recent data, merge them, or prioritize one protocol over another? If both DHCP and DHCPv6 offer DNS servers, which list does the client use?

Different administrative management: In some environments (like community wireless), IPv4 and IPv6 services are managed by different organizations. A client may need to know which configuration came from which source and apply it accordingly.

Multiple interfaces: Some devices have separate IPv4 and IPv6 on different interfaces. The question becomes whether a setting like NTP server is per-interface or per-device, and how to choose among conflicting values.

DNS load balancing: Some sites use DNS round-robin to spread load across servers. If the IPv4 and IPv6 lists come from separate servers without coordinated ordering, load balancing breaks.

DNS search path variations: A site may temporarily use a subdomain (e.g., ipv6.example.com) for IPv6-specific testing. If DHCP and DHCPv6 provide different search paths, name resolution can be inconsistent.

Protocol startup sequence: What if IPv6 starts after IPv4 is already configured? Should the device merge the new information or replace the old?

DHCP option variations: Some options exist only in one protocol. Some sites want lists that contain both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Questions like: What if IPv6 info arrives after IPv4? What if the two servers give different answers? How do you pick which one to use? Can devices with multiple network cards use different settings on each? What if you're trying to balance traffic across servers?

sections.title: Two Proposed Approaches
sections.content:
Separate servers (recommended): Run both DHCP and DHCPv6 servers, possibly on the same machine. Generate their configurations from a single database to ensure consistency (e.g., both servers return the same NTP server address). Clients merge responses using heuristics like "use DHCPv6 first, then DHCPv6, then fall back to DHCP". Sites maintain consistency through administrative discipline and configuration management tools.

Advantages: Simplicity for the protocols themselves; reuses proven DHCP infrastructure; IPv6-only clients are not forced to receive IPv4 information; IPv4-only devices continue to work. Disadvantages: Administrators must manage two servers; merging at the client is complex; information can still be lost if the servers disagree.

Single DHCPv6 server with IPv4 options (not recommended): Extend DHCPv6 to carry IPv4 addresses and configuration, eliminating DHCP entirely for dual-stack nodes. This simplifies clients but creates new problems: IPv4-only devices still need DHCP; if some DHCPv6 servers don't implement IPv4 options, clients are left without service; IPv4 address space must be allocated to both servers, fragmenting precious global addresses; it violates the principle that how you transport data shouldn't affect what kind of addresses you can get.
sections.plainLanguage: Option 1: Keep two servers but make sure they say the same thing, and teach clients how to merge them. Option 2: Put everything in one IPv6 server. The document says Option 1 is better because Option 2 breaks too many things.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 4477 notes that it does not introduce new security issues, as it does not propose a new protocol. However, it observes that both DHCP and DHCPv6 are vulnerable to spoofing because authentication is rarely implemented. Adding a second protocol increases the potential attack surface: an attacker might spoof DHCPv6 but not DHCP (or vice versa), causing clients to receive a mix of legitimate and forged configuration.

This reinforces the importance of keeping configuration synchronized at the administrative level and considering authentication mechanisms where available (such as DHCP authentication defined in RFC 3118).
sections.plainLanguage: Both DHCP protocols can be faked. Having two means twice as many places to attack. Making sure both servers always agree on important information helps reduce the chance that an attacker can inject bad data.

sections.title: Practical Deployment Guidance
sections.content:
The RFC acknowledges that IPv4 DHCP will be required for many years as legacy devices (printers, webcams, older equipment) continue to use DHCPv4. A single DHCPv6 server cannot serve these IPv4-only nodes, so most real deployments will operate both servers indefinitely.

The recommendation is to implement a configuration manager that accepts a single specification from the network operator and distributes the correct configuration to both DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 servers. This reduces administrative burden and ensures consistency. The client's job is then to merge the responses intelligently using best-practice rules.

RFC 4477 notes that deployment experience with DHCPv6 was still early, so full understanding of all issues would develop over time. The consensus position was that the two-server approach was the best pragmatic solution given the current state of the technology.
sections.plainLanguage: In practice, old devices that only speak IPv4 will still be around. So you'll run both servers for a long time. Make a tool that keeps them synchronized from a master list. Let clients merge the results using simple rules.
